question: The Commission is proposing a root-and-branch overhaul of the public procurement market which would see the existing directives replaced by a directly applicable regulation. The proposal does away with the traditional lowest-price criterion and introduces mandatory “quality” criteria with weightings of up to 50 % and direct negotiations between authorities and firms. In practice, these mechanisms could make local projects hugely more expensive and public spending less transparent. 1.

How will the Commission financially offset the inevitable rise in costs for local authorities in less developed regions due to the requirement to introduce social and environmental criteria with weightings of at least 30-50 %?

What specific corruption control mechanisms does the new framework introduce to prevent backroom deals, against the backdrop of the legalisation of direct negotiations between contracting authorities and certain tenderers?

What economic data did the Commission rely on when it concluded that the restriction of competition through the “European preference” clause would not lead to an increase in the end prices paid by taxpayers for large-scale infrastructure projects?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2026) On 9 September 2026, the Commission adopted its proposal for a Public Procurement Act1 to modernise EU public procurement rules. The impacts of policy options supporting strategic procurement have been tested in the Impact Assessment Report2.

That report includes evidence according to which any potential price effects of Best Price Quality Ratio are likely to be limited and context-specific. This evidence is further underpinned by references to research that demonstrates that when measured in terms of total life-cycle costs, strategic procurement measures do not have significant effects on prices.
Furthermore, the proposal introduces the possibility of adaptations in order to meet the specific needs of the public procurement markets of the outermost regions of the EU (Article 144).

The proposed Digital Marketplace, through which all public procurement in scope of the Regulation must be carried out, would ensure transparency and accountability in procurement procedures, acting as a safeguard against potential irregular practices.

The processing of all procurement procedures through the marketplace will allow for AI-supported data analytics to identify risk transactions for in-depth analysis by auditors, prosecutors and competition authorities.

In its assessment of potential price impacts of European preference clauses in public procurement, the Commission relied on in-house sources such as the FIDELIO3 model that estimated macro-economic effects of domestic content requirement in selected sectors of key importance for the EU infrastructure, as well as external studies such as a World Bank study4, that included the analysis of impacts of potential award concentration levels driven by a reduced pool of eligible bidders.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52026PC0590. 2 See section 6.3. of Commission Staff Working Document, Impact Assessment Report, SWD(2026) 591 final,

Brussels, 9.9.2026. 3 The FIDELIO (Full Interregional Dynamic Econometric Long-term Input-Output) is a multi-country general equilibrium model for estimating the socio-economic and environmental impacts of EU industrial, trade, and innovation policies for a fair and sustainable EU economy. It is developed and run by the Joint Research Centre. (https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.

eu/scientific-activities/trade-and-industrial-policy-analysis/industrialpolicy/fidelio-model_en). 4 World Bank. Study on Competition in the European Union’s Public Procurement Markets (2018-2023) (English). Washington, D.C. : World Bank Group, (http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/099111425044525338).
